name: Induced Vertical Break
summary: The up-and-down movement a pitch gets from its spin alone, with gravity taken out. Measured in inches.
easy: No fastball truly rises. A "rising fastball" carries so much backspin that it sinks less than a normal pitch would.

IVB is the size of that missing drop. The more IVB a four-seamer has, the higher it crosses the plate compared with where the hitter expects it, and from the batter's box the ball seems to jump. On a four-seamer, anything over 18 inches is strong ride.

scale.note: For four-seam fastballs. Sinkers and two-seamers work the other way: the less IVB, the better they do their job.

deep: Take the actual path the tracking system measured, subtract the drop due to gravity, and what's left is IVB. Vertical Break, the total drop with gravity left in, is a different stat, so a movement figure without a label could be either one.

Spin rate doesn't decide it alone. How much of a pitch's spin becomes movement (spin efficiency) and which way the axis points matter as well. High-spin four-seamers with nothing-special IVB are common.

myth.claim: Higher spin makes the ball rise more.
myth.truth: If spin efficiency is low, even a high spin rate won't add up to much vertical movement. IVB itself is the more accurate number for ride.

leagues.t: Pitch-level tracking data isn't public in enough detail to confirm IVB from an official source. For import pitchers with MLB experience, their Baseball Savant data is a useful reference.
